<reason>Both sides were disciplined and well-grounded, but B converted the decisive clash. B's core empirical anchor—wealthy states repealing failed wealth taxes—persisted through every round, and when A honestly conceded it "cannot reliably identify a single missing feature" distinguishing its proposal from the repealed systems, B seized that admission in Rebuttal 2 and the closing as the vote-deciding moment. A's counter that "history doesn't strictly disprove it" and political repeal isn't a cost-benefit calculation was coherent but left the "why is this time different" burden substantially unmet. A did land real damage: its pressure questions forced B to concede that tracing debt-financed consumption is "genuinely hard," and A's restricted-deferral answer (annual measurement, safety valve not default) blunted the "functionally an estate tax" attack. But B's "worst of both worlds" reframe—hardest tax on the most mobile base, duplicating estate taxation where illiquid—was the sharper weighing in the late rounds, and B sustained progression rather than repetition. B's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a minor execution cost, as is a slight overreach in treating "cannot reliably identify" as a total admission, but neither outweighs its cleaner path to victory. A wins points on epistemic honesty and reframing the comparison as imperfect-instrument-vs-imperfect-instrument; B wins on the burden question that survived the exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.5–B4.7): B leveraged A's concession that no distinguishing design feature could be identified, then reframed A's restricted-deferral retreat as "the worst of both worlds"—annually taxing the most mobile (liquid) wealth while converting illiquid fortunes into a de facto estate tax plus valuation machinery. This crystallized the burden clash and the instrument-selection weighing that decided the debate.</best_rebuttal>
